Question: Corners are sliced off a unit cube so that the six faces each become regular octagons. What is the total volume of the removed tetrahedra?
Solution:
First examine an original square face. A regular octagon has interior angles
\[
\frac{(8-2)180^\circ}{8}=135^\circ.
\]
Thus each removed corner triangle has angles \(90^\circ,45^\circ,45^\circ\), so its two legs along the square's edges are equal. Equal octagon sides make all four corner triangles on that face congruent. Let their leg length be \(t\).

A new diagonal side of the octagon has length \(t\sqrt2\), by the Pythagorean theorem. A side remaining along an original cube edge has length \(1-2t\). Regularity requires these lengths to agree:
\[
1-2t=t\sqrt2,
\qquad t=\frac{1}{2+\sqrt2}=\frac{2-\sqrt2}{2}.
\]
The same argument applies to every face, so all edge cutbacks have this value.

At each cube vertex, the removed tetrahedron has three mutually perpendicular edges of length \(t\). Choose the right triangular face with area \(t^2/2\) as its base; its height is \(t\). Its volume is therefore
\[
\frac13\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\right)t=\frac{t^3}{6}.
\]
There is one such piece at each of the eight vertices. Since \(0<t<1/2\), these corner pieces are disjoint. Their total volume is
\[
\begin{aligned}
8\cdot\frac{t^3}{6}
&=\frac{(2-\sqrt2)^3}{6}\\
&=\frac{20-14\sqrt2}{6}
=\frac{10-7\sqrt2}{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\dfrac{10-7\sqrt2}{3}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
